items.note: Story 1: Association named, organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president; creamery dated as the year before the 1892 adoption.
Story 1 states Article VII in full: paid by pounds of butterfat by test not weight of milk, and the station's test governs.
Story 1 ties the rule to what a faulty instrument cost: reliability of the test made 'a matter of survival', Gideon 'drafted the clause without understanding what it would cost'.
Only Teague (bookkeeper since 1905) is given a role inside Section A. Loomis and Sill appear in Section A only as narrator credits; their offices are stated in C/D/F, which cannot travel into A.
Section A gives 'Selby Vose, manager since 1913' but never says he was Gideon's son. The son relation is stated only in B3/E5 and cannot travel into A.

Section A's only station-gain statement is the quoted bulletin line identifying the 76,000 lb with the ledger entries; that is A8.6's aspect and is credited there. A1.6's own aspect (origin in 1898, the ~5.25 percent shape) appears only in Section D. Anti-double-scoring rule applied.
Story 2: skimming station, seven miles up the valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896, glassware borrowed from Larrow Green.

Partial but core mechanism present in A: pounds recorded in the test book, and Story 7's 'short charge of milk into a bottle whose neck is ruled for a full one yields a reading short in the same proportion'. Composite sampling and the skim return are missing.
Story 2: ordered from Ammon & Sons, Tarnet; invoice 14 April 1897; in use 1 May 1897.
Story 2 gives 6 dozen pipettes marked 17.6 c.c., 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, $77.93 including freight.
Story 8 states the 'nineteen hundredths' gap 'stood flat every month'; Story 3 adds July and February alike, wet years and dry.
Never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette, and asserts the contrary background (the state issued burettes from 1921 and Strawn carried one on his rounds).
Ansel Keddie, twenty-nine seasons from the 1896 opening, dismissed 30 April 1925, died 1934. (Run's 'a man of fifty-five' in 1896 is its own slip: canon has him b. 1861.)
Story 2: five columns date, patron, pounds, test, fat, in his own hand, errors crossed and initialed, never written over.
Both figures inside Section A: 3.61 from 1898 onward, and 3.80 as 'the level Ansel had recorded for 1896, the first year on borrowed glass'.
Story 3: pipette broke 8 May 1911, borrowed measure to 10 July, nine weeks at 3.80, back to 3.61 the day the station's measure returned, question mark recorded.
Story 4: Emmet Brant is 'Ansel's brother-in-law, the largest patron of the station, and Orra's brother'.
Story 4 has the 1919 water circular over Vose's signature; Story 6 has Keddie's 17 March 1925 statement (tested as taught, never took a pound of cream, cannot say why the figures are what they are).
Died 1934, still under the stigma of dismissal (Story 6). Bolded element present.
Six farms of Hessel Bottom (Story 2); wet meadow under water every spring (Story 3); Emmet Brant the largest patron (Story 4).
Brant's weigh book and the two agreeing scales appear only in C2 and in the Kyle quote in Section F. Nothing in Section A.

Complaints from 1902 are present, but Story 3 fuses the two gaps: it computes Larrow Green 3.78 against 3.61 and then calls the difference '0.17 to 0.19 points'. The key gates this item on keeping the Hollow-vs-Green 0.17 apart from the 0.19 shortfall.
Story 3: Grigg's 1908 committee sampled January, February and March and concluded the wet hay thinned the cream, reported as the committee's finding, not as fact.
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in Section C2; proportionality of the loss only in Section F. Neither is in Section A.
No mention of the weigh book passing to Roy Brant in 1929 or being lent to Ivy in 1958. Hazel Brant appears only as a narrator credit.
Alder Corners appears exactly once in the whole sheet, in Section F. Nothing in Section A; no credit travels into A.
The four summer-flush haulers from 1915 are named only in Section F.
The independence of the Alder Corners test is argued only in Section F ('different (correct) glassware'), not in Section A.
The sixteen-season 0.19 overlap is stated only in Section F.
The same-milk-two-buildings argument is made only in Section F.
Rosalie Cudd named only in Section F, and only as the source of 'data'; no daughter relation, no 1958 copying.

Story 5: Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector for the Ordell circuit, 1907-1936. (Elsewhere the sheet contradicts itself with 1908; that takes a corruption deduction but the bolded 1907-1936 is present here.)
Story 4: tested for water at every visit and never found any; Story 5: 'finding scales true, no water, and honest work' across twenty-six years of visits.
Story 5: on 12 June 1923 he ran the station's pipettes against his calibrated burette and condemned the whole crate.
Story 5: 'he did not weigh what it had cost them'; made no inference about the twenty-six years of tests.
Story 5: ordered 28 June, Ammon reply 2 July 1923, new glass in use by July; 1924 average rose to 3.80; nobody connected the rise to the condemnation. Correct 3.80, not r08's 3.90.

Story 7: the crate 'had lain there since June 12, 1923, the day it was condemned' in the loft above the intake room. (The notebooks' 1947 move to the college library is absent, but the crate-in-1923 aspect is this item's own.)
Story 6: the patrons petitioned in January 1925. Attribution to the standing grievance rather than the 1924 rise is expressly allowed.
Board under Alonzo Frick, first session 17 March, award 4 May 1925, three sessions, two of them at the station itself.
Three explanations, none accepted: watering (Selby Vose), the tester's theft (Wilbur Teague), the bog hay (Grigg's 1908 report read into the record); board found 'no cause established'.
The four-book exhibit list appears only in the Kyle quotation in Section F. Section A says only that the board 'examined scales and books'.
Dismissed 30 April 1925 without a finding, four days before the award of $3,800 'without admission' on 4 May 1925.
Section A never says the award was one fifth of the loss nor that it was charged to the station-gain account. Only '$19,000 ... The patrons received $3,800' as adjacent sentences.
Ivy Keddie, graduate student in dairy husbandry at the State Agricultural College at Farland, Ansel's granddaughter through Duncan; Vaught named in Story 8.
No account of assembling records that had never been in one room. Section A has only the crate and the bulletin; the Alder Corners figures are absent from Section A entirely.
February 1958, crate found in the station loft, nine of the original seventy-two pipettes surviving.
9 March 1958, five deliveries each against a calibrated burette, mean 16.72 c.c. against a marked 17.6, short 0.88 c.c., 0.95 of the mark.
Story 7 and the Story 8 bulletin quote: every test from 1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 low by one part in twenty, 3.61 recorded where 3.80 stood, gap 0.19.

REQUIRED all four present in Section A: 40 million lb over 25 full years, 76,000 lb of fat, $19,000 at 25 cents, and the bulletin quote identifying the same 76,000 lb with the 'station gain' standing in the Association's own ledgers.
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, states the cause and clears him; 'dead twenty-four years' given.
Granddaughter.
Ivy is Duncan's daughter, Duncan is Ansel's son, with Duncan's own statement quoted.
Second cousins, derived correctly: Roy and Duncan are first cousins as the children of a brother and sister, so Hazel and Ivy are the children of first cousins.

Abstention item A08 not engaged at all. The run raises a different open question (whether Emmet had other children) and never says the full-or-half sibling question is unsettleable or that it does not change the answer. No definite assertion either, so no gullibility deduction.
Gideon Vose, his father; Kyle's correction of the 'nephew' version quoted.
States that Gideon wrote Article VII making the station's test decide every patron's pay, and links it to Selby's management and his water accusation.
Asserts a verdict: 'I resolve in favor of no blood relationship.' The key's operational test makes this an assertion, not an abstention. -2 applied in deductions.
Lays out what is on the record: Oram's cousinship from talk, hedged and second-hand, against Duncan's flat family denial; no paper cited on either side.
Headline answer correct: tests low by exactly 5 percent, one part in twenty. (The stated ratio 0.9524 is an arithmetic slip; 16.72/17.6 is exactly 0.95, and the slip is what wrecks C2.)
True average 3.80, short by 0.19.
$19,000 at 25 cents; $3,800 received; one fifth / 20 percent. Both money and fraction given.
Wrong. Divides by the bad 0.9524 and gets a true test of 3.59 and 340 lb owed. Key requires 3.60 and 360 lb (200,000 x 3.60 percent = 7,200 less 6,840).
Wrong. $85 from the bad 340 lb. Key requires $86.40 (360 x $0.24), or $90.00 only with an explicit statement that the period average is being used.
1,444,000 lb credited.
1,520,000 lb actually delivered.
76,000 lb, given both ways with denominators named: 5.0 percent of fat delivered, 5.26 percent of fat credited. Avoids the NT-20 trap.
All five line items and $77.93.
72 pipettes (6 dozen), each short 0.88 c.c. Both elements.

Gives '26 years and 1 month'. Exact-match item: the key wants 26 years and 6 weeks (or 26 years 42 days / 26 years 1 month 11 days). The 25 full years 1898-1922 and the reason for the difference are correct, but the first figure is not an exact equivalent.
Abstention A02 honored: 'not precisely recorded in extant accounts', both memory figures given without choosing, and Section E says flatly 'Cannot be determined from sources'. No deduction.
Variable named as the pipette; broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July 1911.
Constants listed well beyond three: patrons, herds, pasture and season, operator, acid, bottles, hand tester.
3.80 through the nine weeks, back to 3.61 the same day the station's measure returned.

Both halves. Establishes apparatus over herds/land/feed, and (via D2 reason 1, creditable anywhere in B-G) over the tester's honesty; and states limits: the interval does not say what is wrong with the measure or by how much.
Three reasons, each attributed: the 1911 interval (Keddie's test book), Sill's receiving book, the station-gain ledger line (Teague).

The independence demonstration is wrong. Reasons 2 and 3 rest on the same event, the Ostrey Hollow cream arriving heavy at Larrow Green (Sill weighs it, Teague books it), so the explicit 'these three reasons do not depend on one another' fails the key's test of no two resting on the same document, witness or event. The second half (one reason surviving without the 1958 measurement) is done.
Abstention A09 asserted: 'So yes, Teague questioned the entries once (in 1916), was rebuffed, and asked no more.' The rival account (he never asked anybody anything) is never mentioned. -2 applied.
Answers the literal question yes, with the 1919 circular and the ledger sheets as support.
REQUIRED three of five: manager from 1913, signed the annual ledger sheets carrying the station-gain line, wrote the 1919 water circular.

Abstention A03 asserted. Headline verdict sentence: 'Yes, the manager knew before June 12, 1923, and is likely to have understood that the glass might be faulty.' Later 'less certain' hedging does not undo a verdict sentence, and nothing declares the question unsettleable. -2 applied.

Kyle's 1922 against 12 June 1923 (planted error X96): found, resolved to 12 June 1923, method stated (contemporaneous circuit-book entry plus the 28 June order letter, against a memory thirty years later).

Great-niece against granddaughter (NT-18) resolved correctly with method (family record plus r22's own closing correction). E-a only, not E-b: the run misnames the carriers as Nym/Kyle/Falke/Oram instead of r19 and r22.
Nephew against son (NT-17) resolved correctly with method (Kyle's explicit correction, family knowledge). E-a only: just one carrier (r12) named, so the pair is not broken as a pair.
E-a capped at 3; no further eligible resolutions offered.

NT-10 broken as a pair: Claim C (Kyle r23) and Claim D (Vaught r11) both carry 1 May 1898, and the tie is broken by the 14 April 1897 invoice and Orra's contemporaneous diary, with the priority rule stated.
No other pair broken as a pair. NT-1 is not merely missed but swallowed: Story 5 asserts 16.27 c.c. NT-11 (12 July), NT-14 ($77.39), NT-20 and NT-19 are not raised as pairs.

None of A04, A06 or A10 declared unsettleable. A04 is asserted (a mold shifted or worn), A10 is asserted (adopted 1892), A06 is hedged in a parenthesis but never identified as an open question. Contradiction 4 (the 1896 intake) is correctly abstained but is A02, scored at C5b, not an E-c row.

No narrator caught refuting itself on the page. The nearest thing, Falke's own footnote correction, is a narrator correcting himself deliberately, not an internal self-refutation the solver detected. Several of the sheet's own 'contradictions' (6, 8, 10) are non-conflicts padded into the list.

Cause and size: the 1897 crate's pipettes, 16.72 against 17.6, 95 percent of truth, proportional so 0.19 is 5 percent of 3.80; onset on the 1896 borrowed-glass 3.80 and cessation on the 1923 condemnation and 1924 return to 3.80, with nothing on the farms changing.
Watering named (Vose, 1919 circular and 1926 address) and defeated with Strawn's lactometer, Sill's heavy cream and the 1911 interval.
Theft named (Teague's 1925 argument) and defeated specifically: the cream arrived heavy, not light, in the accuser's own ledger, plus the 1911 interval under the same tester.

Bog hay named (Grigg's 1908 committee, Kepp) and defeated with Bulletin 214 quoted correctly at five hundredths in winter and nothing in summer, the flat month-to-month 0.19, and the Alder Corners comparison.
Abstention A07 asserted. The answer opens 'No.' and argues the board never examined the glass. Leaning that way while declining would have been fine; a flat verdict is not. -2 applied.

Abstention A05 asserted. Adopts the son's 'it is something in the glass' as fact and concludes 'Ansel suspected the glass might be faulty'; the chairman's opposite recollection is never mentioned. -2 applied.
147 words by count, within the 150 cap.

Only Article VII (by-laws) and the 1958 measurement are identifiable record series. No invoice, test book, weigh book, Alder Corners book, Strawn notebooks, arbitration minutes or ledgers. Far short of five.
Clean. All three decoys named as false theories, no wrong headline number: 5 percent, 0.19, $3,800, 1897, 1923 crate, 1958, Bulletin 471.

Four of six arc elements with both ends covered: short by 5 percent, running from 1897 (onset), explained in 1958 (close), and both Keddies named. Missing the 76,000 lb / $19,000 and the 1923 condemnation date.

deductions.reason: Corruption: asserts the planted 16.27 c.c. as fact in Story 5 ('when tested, they delivered approximately 16.27 cubic centimeters'), unhedged, and in flat contradiction of its own correct 16.72 in Story 7

Corruption: asserts Strawn's circuit beginning in 1908 (NT-23) as fact twice - Story 4 'at every visit from 1908 onward' and F2 'from 1908 to 1936 (29 years)' - even though Story 5 gives the correct 1907-1936
Gullibility A01: resolves the Vose-Keddie kinship question - 'I resolve in favor of no blood relationship'
Gullibility A03: headline verdict that Vose 'is likely to have understood that the glass might be faulty'; no declared inability to settle the understatement question

Gullibility A04: asserts the accident pole for the short lot - the pipettes 'were manufactured with a mold that had shifted or worn', 'a systematic manufacturing error' - where the sources settle nothing (Ammon's works records burned in 1931)
Gullibility A05: asserts what the tester believed, adopting Duncan's 'it is something in the glass' as fact and concluding 'Ansel suspected the glass might be faulty'
Gullibility A07: answers 'No.' to whether the 1925 board examined the condemned glassware
Gullibility A09: answers 'So yes, Teague questioned the entries once (in 1916)' on whether the bookkeeper ever queried the station-gain line
Gullibility A10: asserts Article VII was 'adopted at the annual meeting in 1892', settling the unsettleable year payment by butterfat began
